title: Electrons Hopping across a Molecular Network: Spectra and Symmetries
authors: Ludwig Schulz, Max Best, Carsten Henkel
abstract: We investigate interacting spinless electrons on finite molecular ring networks described by a tight-binding Hubbard Hamiltonian. The interplay between lattice geometry, Coulomb interactions and discrete symmetries is analysed for rings with $L=3,4,5,6$ nodes, filled with one, two or three electrons. Special attention is devoted to the role of the network symmetries in determining the structure of the many-body spectrum and the Mulliken classification of the eigenstates. Using group-theoretical methods, we examine the evolution of the spectra in the presence of an external magnetic flux. The Zeeman effect lifts degeneracies and results in combination with the Coulomb interaction to avoided crossings in symmetry sectors. We identify a qualitatively distinction between systems with an even and odd number of particles. At half-filling, particle-hole symmetry (duality) protects selected symmetry sectors against Zeeman splitting.
summary: This paper theoretically investigates the energy spectra of interacting spinless electrons on finite molecular rings using a Hubbard model. It leverages group theory and symmetry analysis to predict spectral features, such as avoided crossings due to magnetic flux and the protection of certain states by particle-hole symmetry at half-filling.
main_problem: The study investigates how lattice geometry, Coulomb interactions, and discrete symmetries govern the many-body energy spectrum of interacting spinless electrons on molecular ring networks.
main_result: The analysis reveals qualitative differences in spectra based on whether the number of particles is even or odd, and demonstrates that particle-hole symmetry protects certain spectral sectors from Zeeman splitting at half-filling.
method: Group-theoretical methods are employed to analyze symmetries (using $C_L$ and $D_L$), leading to state classification into irreducible representations. The spectrum is calculated using a tight-binding Hubbard Hamiltonian, often requiring the construction of effective Hamiltonians for coupled symmetry sectors.
model_or_system: The system models interacting spinless electrons on finite molecular ring networks (size L), governed by a tight-binding Hubbard Hamiltonian incorporating hopping ($t_{st}$), on-site repulsion ($U$), and two-body interactions ($V_{st}$). The effects of an external magnetic flux ($\Phi$) are included via Peierls substitution.
key_observables: Many-body spectrum (energy eigenvalues), persistent current, magnetization, and the splitting/avoided crossing patterns as a function of magnetic flux $\Phi$.
important_parameters: Lattice size L ($3 \le L \le 6$), number of electrons N (1, 2, or 3), external magnetic flux $\Phi$, and interaction strengths $U$ and $V_{st}$.
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes spinless fermions obeying the Pauli principle. The use of group theory heavily constrains the possible spectral degeneracies and splittings.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate typical features of ring networks, Zeeman spectra for small rings ($L=3$), flux-dependent energy levels showing avoided crossings, and scaling plots comparing Coulomb energy across different lattice geometries.
paper_structure: The paper systematically analyzes the Hamiltonian using group theory to classify states. It then examines how external fields (Zeeman effect) and interactions cause spectral changes, paying special attention to symmetry protection mechanisms like particle-hole duality at half-filling.
why_interesting: This work provides a detailed theoretical framework for understanding how fundamental symmetries dictate electronic behavior in low-dimensional quantum materials, which is highly relevant to designing correlated quantum devices or simulating molecular electronics.

figures.caption: Figure 1. Typical features of ring networks. Left: mirror axes and elementary rotation for an even number of sites. Right: sign of hopping matrix elements. The amplitudes for an electron hopping from site 1 to neighboring sites may have opposite signs. After the hop 1 →5 across the “ring-closing” edge (red barrier), a reordering is needed to restore the canonical ordering of creation operators. This leads to a minus sign if there is an odd number of other electrons on the ring.
Figure 2. Zeeman spectrum for triangular ring with (left) one and (right) two electrons.

Figure 3. Left: Zeeman spectrum for a square with two electrons. Thick (thin) lines denote two-fold (singly) degenerate levels. We subtract the mean Coulomb interaction VC(2). The irreps B1 + A2 remain degenerate because they are dual to each other (half-filled network). Gray lines indicate energy levels without Coulomb interaction. For the symmetry assignment in the right column, a total momentum −1 has been subtracted. Right: network geometry with its generating symmetry elements. For each type σv and σd, there are two equivalent mirror axes.

Figure 4. Left: Zeeman spectrum for a pentagon ring with two electrons. The line thickness indicates the degeneracy (single or double). Gray lines indicate the spectra without Coulomb interaction. Note the avoided crossing between two E−2 terms, while levels with different symmetries cross. Right: network geometry and its symmetry elements. Five other equivalent σv axes exist.

Figure 5. Same as Figs. 3, 4 for a hexagonal ring with three electrons. Note the doubly degenerate levels (thick lines, E1 and E2): their splitting is forbidden by duality which exchanges the two momentum components.
